newsitem.title: UK: UK Consumer credit seen backing stronger economy.
newsitem.headline: UK Consumer credit seen backing stronger economy.

text.p: British consumer credit data for September confirm the economy is strengthening and add further fuel to the case for higher interest rates, analysts said.
They said the figures, released earlier on Tuesday, suggest consumer spending and retail sales will be even more robust in the run up to Christmas.
"This is a gale warning for the British economy," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
"It will strengthen the Governor of the Bank of England's feeling that interest rates are too low."
Consumer credit rose to 1.067 billion pounds ($1.72 billion) in September from an upwardly revised 1.044 billion in August.
"Credit data has been telling us for many months that UK consumer's attitude towards debt has not changed significantly for the last four to five years," said Gardiner.

"As the housing market gathers momentum, we'll see total consumer borrowing accelerate quiet markedly and with the broad money supply already growing at roughly 10 percent, it's very difficult to see a significant slow-down in the ammount of liquidity sloshing around the economy," he said.
Andrew Snowball, Treasury economist at Cooperative Bank, said the figures showed growth at 2.3 percent in the third quarter was accelerating.

"It gives clear evidence that the economy is picking up pretty fast," he said. "It is another piece of evidence the Governor (of the Bank of England) might point to...for possibly tighter monetary policy."

The value of mortgage, or home loan, approvals was 5.985 billion pounds for September, compared with 5.879 billion in August and 4.431 billion a year ago. The number of approvals stood at 94,000 compared with 90,000 in the previous month.

"These figures continue to show signs of a steady recovery in the housing market, but that there may be some fluctuations from month to month," said Adrian Coles, director general at the Council of Mortgage Lenders.
"The fact that approvals continue to run at a high level is encouraging for lending during the remainder of 1996 and into 1997."
Bank of England Governor Eddie George and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke hold their monthly monetary policy meeting on Wednesday.

George has been pressing for official interest rates to be increased to six percent from their current 5.75 level, but with a general election only months away, the Chancellor is expected to hold fire despite the credit data.
"The Chancellor will hold George off at least in the short-term because there are still a few things he can point at, most of all the rise in sterling in recent months," said Snowball.

Analysts said the currency's appreciation is effectively doing the job of higher interest rates. As a rough guide, a four percent appreciation in sterling is equivalent to a one percentage point increase in base rates.
